===Etymology===
{{root|en|ine-pro|*dʰegʷʰ-}}
From {{inh|en|enm|Saterday}}, from {{inh|en|ang|sæterdæġ}}, earlier {{m|ang|sæternesdæġ|t=Saterday|lit=Saturn's day}}, from {{inh|en|gmw-pro|*Sāturnas dag}}; a translation of {{der|en|la|diēs Saturnī}}, equivalent to {{af|en|Saturn|day}}. {{ety|en|:inh|enm:to<id:infinitive>}}
From {{inh|en|enm|to||also, in addition to}}, from {{inh|en|ang|tō||furthermore, also, besides}}, adverbial use of preposition {{m|ang|tō||to, into}}. The sense of "in addition, also" deriving from the original meaning of "apart, separately" (compare Old English prefix {{m|ang|tō-||apart}}). {{doublet|en|to}}; see there for more.

And, as their ubiquity spreads, so '''too''' does the debate around whether we should allow ourselves to become so reliant on them – and who, if anyone, is policing their use.}}

====Usage notes====
* Used in the conjunctive sense, ''too'' is used [[Appendix:Glossary#postpositive|postpositive]]ly, often offset with a pause (in speaking) or commas (in writing), and pronounced with {{w|phrasal stress}}.
* When used in their senses as degree adverbs, ''[[very]]'' and ''too'' never modify verbs; ''[[very much]]'' and ''[[too much]]'' do instead.

==English== ===Alternative forms=== * {{alt|en|larn||Northumbrian}} * {{alt|en|learne||obsolete}} ===Etymology=== {{etymon|en|:inh|enm:lernen>}} From {{inh|en|enm|lernen|t=to learn", also, "to teach"}}, from {{inh|en|ang|leornian|t=to learn", rarely also, "to teach}}, from {{inh|en|gmw-pro|*liʀnōn}}, from {{inh|en|gem-pro|*lizaną}}, from {{inh|en|ine-pro||*(le-)lóys-e}}, stative from the root {{m|ine-pro|*leys-|t=track, furrow, trace, trail}}. The spelling with ⟨ea⟩ is of {{w|Early Modern English}} origin and reflects a lengthening of {{IPAchar|/ɛ~e/}} to {{IPAfont|/eː/}} before {{IPAchar|/rn/}} in Late Old English or Early Middle English, then later lowering to {{IPAchar|/ɛː/}}; the modern pronunciation reflects still later reshortening.
